564:     /// Attempt to do a fast confirmation of a word match that covers a subset
565:     /// (but hopefully a big subset) of most cases. Ok(Some(..)) is returned
566:     /// when a match is found. Ok(None) is returned when there is definitively
567:     /// no match. Err(()) is returned when this routine could not detect
568:     /// whether there was a match or not.
569:     fn fast_find(
570:         &self,
571:         haystack: &[u8],
572:         at: usize,
573:     ) -> Result<Option<Match>, ()> {
574:         // This is a bit hairy. The whole point here is to avoid running a
575:         // slower regex engine to extract capture groups. Remember, our word
576:         // regex looks like this:
577:         //
578:         //     (^|\W)(<original regex>)(\W|$)
579:         //
580:         // What we want are the match offsets of <original regex>. So in the
581:         // easy/common case, the original regex will be sandwiched between
582:         // two codepoints that are in the \W class. So our approach here is to
583:         // look for a match of the overall word regexp, strip the \W ends and
584:         // then check whether the original regex matches what's left. If so,
585:         // then we are guaranteed a correct match.
586:         //
587:         // This only works though if we know that the match is sandwiched
588:         // between two \W codepoints. This only occurs when neither ^ nor $
589:         // match. This in turn only occurs when the match is at either the
590:         // beginning or end of the haystack. In either of those cases, we
591:         // declare defeat and defer to the slower implementation.
592:         //
593:         // The reason why we cannot handle the ^/$ cases here is because we
594:         // can't assume anything about the original pattern. (Try commenting
595:         // out the checks for ^/$ below and run the tests to see examples.)
596:         let input = Input::new(haystack).span(at..haystack.len());
597:         let mut cand = match self.regex.find(input) {
598:             None => return Ok(None),
599:             Some(m) => Match::new(m.start(), m.end()),
600:         };
601:         if cand.start() == 0 || cand.end() == haystack.len() {
602:             return Err(());
603:         }
604:         let (_, slen) = bstr::decode_utf8(&haystack[cand]);
605:         let (_, elen) = bstr::decode_last_utf8(&haystack[cand]);
606:         let new_start = cand.start() + slen;
607:         let new_end = cand.end() - elen;
608:         // This occurs the original regex can match the empty string. In this
609:         // case, just bail instead of trying to get it right here since it's
610:         // likely a pathological case.
611:         if new_start > new_end {
612:             return Err(());
613:         }
614:         cand = cand.with_start(new_start).with_end(new_end);
615:         if self.original.is_match(&haystack[cand]) {
616:             Ok(Some(cand))
617:         } else {
618:             Err(())
619:         }
620:     }

703:     fn renumber_capture_indices(hir: Hir) -> Result<Hir, Error> {
704:         Ok(match hir.into_kind() {
705:             HirKind::Empty => Hir::empty(),
706:             HirKind::Literal(hir::Literal(lit)) => Hir::literal(lit),
707:             HirKind::Class(cls) => Hir::class(cls),
708:             HirKind::Look(x) => Hir::look(x),
709:             HirKind::Repetition(mut x) => {
710:                 x.sub = Box::new(Self::renumber_capture_indices(*x.sub)?);
711:                 Hir::repetition(x)
712:             }
713:             HirKind::Capture(mut cap) => {
714:                 cap.index = match cap.index.checked_add(1) {
715:                     Some(index) => index,
716:                     None => {
717:                         let msg = "could not renumber capture index, too big";
718:                         return Err(Error::any(msg));
719:                     }
720:                 };
721:                 cap.sub = Box::new(Self::renumber_capture_indices(*cap.sub)?);
722:                 Hir::capture(cap)
723:             }
724:             HirKind::Concat(subs) => {
725:                 let subs = subs
726:                     .into_iter()
727:                     .map(Self::renumber_capture_indices)
728:                     .collect::<Result<Vec<Hir>, Error>>()?;
729:                 Hir::concat(subs)
730:             }
731:             HirKind::Alternation(subs) => {
732:                 let subs = subs
733:                     .into_iter()
734:                     .map(Self::renumber_capture_indices)
735:                     .collect::<Result<Vec<Hir>, Error>>()?;
736:                 Hir::alternation(subs)
737:             }
738:         })
739:     }

    ///
    /// The original regex is in the capture group at index 1.
    pub(crate) fn regex(&self) -> &Regex {
        &self.regex
    }

    /// Return the underlying HIR for the regex used to match at word
    /// boundaries.
    pub(crate) fn chir(&self) -> &ConfiguredHIR {
        &self.chir
    }

    /// Attempt to do a fast confirmation of a word match that covers a subset
    /// (but hopefully a big subset) of most cases. Ok(Some(..)) is returned
    /// when a match is found. Ok(None) is returned when there is definitively
    /// no match. Err(()) is returned when this routine could not detect
    /// whether there was a match or not.
    fn fast_find(
        &self,
        haystack: &[u8],
        at: usize,
    ) -> Result<Option<Match>, ()> {
        // This is a bit hairy. The whole point here is to avoid running a
        // slower regex engine to extract capture groups. Remember, our word
        // regex looks like this:
        //
        //     (^|\W)(<original regex>)(\W|$)
        //
        // What we want are the match offsets of <original regex>. So in the
        // easy/common case, the original regex will be sandwiched between
        // two codepoints that are in the \W class. So our approach here is to
        // look for a match of the overall word regexp, strip the \W ends and
        // then check whether the original regex matches what's left. If so,
        // then we are guaranteed a correct match.
        //
        // This only works though if we know that the match is sandwiched
        // between two \W codepoints. This only occurs when neither ^ nor $
        // match. This in turn only occurs when the match is at either the
        // beginning or end of the haystack. In either of those cases, we
        // declare defeat and defer to the slower implementation.
        //
        // The reason why we cannot handle the ^/$ cases here is because we
        // can't assume anything about the original pattern. (Try commenting
        // out the checks for ^/$ below and run the tests to see examples.)
        let input = Input::new(haystack).span(at..haystack.len());
        let mut cand = match self.regex.find(input) {
            None => return Ok(None),
            Some(m) => Match::new(m.start(), m.end()),
        };
        if cand.start() == 0 || cand.end() == haystack.len() {
            return Err(());
        }
        let (_, slen) = bstr::decode_utf8(&haystack[cand]);
        let (_, elen) = bstr::decode_last_utf8(&haystack[cand]);
        let new_start = cand.start() + slen;
        let new_end = cand.end() - elen;
        // This occurs the original regex can match the empty string. In this
        // case, just bail instead of trying to get it right here since it's
        // likely a pathological case.
        if new_start > new_end {
            return Err(());
        }
        cand = cand.with_start(new_start).with_end(new_end);
        if self.original.is_match(&haystack[cand]) {
            Ok(Some(cand))
        } else {
            Err(())
        }
    }

    fn ascii_word_byte(b: u8) -> bool {
        if b > 127 {
            false
        } else if b.is_ascii_alphanumeric() {
            true
        } else {
            b == b'_'
        }
    }

    fn utf8_char_width(b: u8) -> usize {
        if b < 0x80 {
            1
        } else if b < 0xE0 {
            2
        } else if b < 0xF0 {
            3
        } else {
            4
        }
    }

    pub(crate) fn wrap_pattern_as_word(
        chir: ConfiguredHIR,
    ) -> Result<ConfiguredHIR, Error> {
        let config = chir.config().clone();
        let mut non_word_config = config.clone();
        non_word_config.fixed_strings = false;
        let non_word = non_word_config.build_many(&[r"\W"])?;
        let line_anchor_start = Hir::look(Self::line_anchor_start(&config));
        let line_anchor_end = Hir::look(Self::line_anchor_end(&config));
        let hir = Hir::concat(vec![
            Hir::alternation(vec![line_anchor_start, non_word.hir().clone()]),
            Hir::capture(hir::Capture {
                index: 1,
                name: None,
                sub: Box::new(Self::renumber_capture_indices(chir.hir().clone())?),
            }),
            Hir::alternation(vec![non_word.hir().clone(), line_anchor_end]),
        ]);
        Ok(ConfiguredHIR::assemble(config, hir))
    }

    pub(crate) fn wrap_whole_line(chir: ConfiguredHIR) -> ConfiguredHIR {
        let config = chir.config().clone();
        let line_anchor_start = Hir::look(Self::line_anchor_start(&config));
        let line_anchor_end = Hir::look(Self::line_anchor_end(&config));
        let hir = Hir::concat(vec![
            line_anchor_start,
            chir.hir().clone(),
            line_anchor_end,
        ]);
        ConfiguredHIR::assemble(config, hir)
    }

    pub(crate) fn anchor_pattern(chir: ConfiguredHIR) -> ConfiguredHIR {
        let config = chir.config().clone();
        let hir = Hir::concat(vec![

            chir.hir().clone(),
            Hir::look(hir::Look::End),
        ]);
        ConfiguredHIR::assemble(config, hir)
    }

    fn renumber_capture_indices(hir: Hir) -> Result<Hir, Error> {
        Ok(match hir.into_kind() {
            HirKind::Empty => Hir::empty(),
            HirKind::Literal(hir::Literal(lit)) => Hir::literal(lit),
            HirKind::Class(cls) => Hir::class(cls),
            HirKind::Look(x) => Hir::look(x),
            HirKind::Repetition(mut x) => {
                x.sub = Box::new(Self::renumber_capture_indices(*x.sub)?);
                Hir::repetition(x)
            }
            HirKind::Capture(mut cap) => {
                cap.index = match cap.index.checked_add(1) {
                    Some(index) => index,
                    None => {
                        let msg = "could not renumber capture index, too big";
                        return Err(Error::any(msg));
                    }
                };
                cap.sub = Box::new(Self::renumber_capture_indices(*cap.sub)?);
                Hir::capture(cap)
            }
            HirKind::Concat(subs) => {
                let subs = subs
                    .into_iter()
                    .map(Self::renumber_capture_indices)
                    .collect::<Result<Vec<Hir>, Error>>()?;
                Hir::concat(subs)
            }
            HirKind::Alternation(subs) => {
                let subs = subs
                    .into_iter()
                    .map(Self::renumber_capture_indices)
                    .collect::<Result<Vec<Hir>, Error>>()?;
                Hir::alternation(subs)
            }
        })
    }

309:     /// does not touch the `crlf` setting.

311:         if yes {

767: /// Represents the match offsets of each capturing group in a match.
768: ///
769: /// The first, or `0`th capture group, always corresponds to the entire match
770: /// and is guaranteed to be present when a match occurs. The next capture
771: /// group, at index `1`, corresponds to the first capturing group in the regex,
772: /// ordered by the position at which the left opening parenthesis occurs.
773: ///
774: /// Note that not all capturing groups are guaranteed to be present in a match.
775: /// For example, in the regex, `(?P<foo>\w)|(?P<bar>\W)`, only one of `foo`
776: /// or `bar` will ever be set in any given match.
777: ///
778: /// In order to access a capture group by name, you'll need to first find the
779: /// index of the group using the corresponding matcher's `capture_index`
780: /// method, and then use that index with `RegexCaptures::get`.
781: #[derive(Clone, Debug)]
782: pub struct RegexCaptures {
783:     /// Where the captures are stored.
784:     caps: AutomataCaptures,
785:     /// These captures behave as if the capturing groups begin at the given
786:     /// offset. When set to `0`, this has no affect and capture groups are
787:     /// indexed like normal.
788:     ///
789:     /// This is useful when building matchers that wrap arbitrary regular
790:     /// expressions. For example, `WordMatcher` takes an existing regex
791:     /// `re` and creates `(?:^|\W)(re)(?:$|\W)`, but hides the fact that
792:     /// the regex has been wrapped from the caller. In order to do this,
793:     /// the matcher and the capturing groups must behave as if `(re)` is
794:     /// the `0`th capture group.
795:     offset: usize,
796: }
797: 
798: impl Captures for RegexCaptures {
799:     fn len(&self) -> usize {
800:         self.caps
801:             .group_info()
802:             .all_group_len()
803:             .checked_sub(self.offset)
804:             .unwrap()
805:     }
806: 
807:     fn get(&self, i: usize) -> Option<Match> {
808:         let actual = i.checked_add(self.offset).unwrap();
809:         self.caps.get_group(actual).map(|sp| Match::new(sp.start, sp.end))
810:     }
811: }
812: 
813: impl RegexCaptures {
814:     pub(crate) fn new(caps: AutomataCaptures) -> RegexCaptures {
815:         RegexCaptures::with_offset(caps, 0)
816:     }
817: 
818:     pub(crate) fn with_offset(
819:         caps: AutomataCaptures,
820:         offset: usize,
821:     ) -> RegexCaptures {
822:         RegexCaptures { caps, offset }
823:     }
824: 
825:     pub(crate) fn captures_mut(&mut self) -> &mut AutomataCaptures {
826:         &mut self.caps
827:     }
828: }
